# llm-usage-extraction

Reads token usage from the session logs that AI coding agents write on your machine, and optionally from Cursor's usage dashboard. Shared by [tokenmaxxing](https://github.com/HansKristoffer/tokenmaxxing) and [agentgate](https://github.com/HansKristoffer/agentgate). Bun only.

| Source          | Where it reads                                                                                                                                                                       |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `claude_code`   | `~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl` (`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`) and PostHog Desktop's `<posthog>/claude/projects`                                                                              |
| `claude_cowork` | Claude Desktop's local agent sessions (`CLAUDE_COWORK_DIR`)                                                                                                                          |
| `codex`         | `~/.codex/sessions/` and `archived_sessions/` (`CODEX_HOME`), the rollouts listed in `state_*.sqlite` (`CODEX_SQLITE_HOME`), and PostHog Desktop's `<posthog>/codex-home/*/sessions` |
| `cursor_local`  | Cursor's `state.vscdb` (`CURSOR_DATA_DIR`) and agent transcripts (`CURSOR_PROJECTS_DIR`)                                                                                             |
| `cursor_api`    | Cursor's usage dashboard, signed in with the token in `state.vscdb`. Opt-in                                                                                                          |
| `grok_bot`      | Grok Bot's rows on that same dashboard. Opt-in                                                                                                                                       |
| `opencode`      | OpenCode's `opencode.db` and `opencode-<channel>.db` in `$XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode` (or `~/.local/share/opencode`, on every OS), and `OPENCODE_DB`                                     |

App data lives in `~/Library/Application Support` on macOS, `%APPDATA%` on Windows and `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` (or `~/.config`) on Linux. `<posthog>` is `@posthog/posthog-code` there, or `POSTHOG_DESKTOP_DIR`.

`cursor_api` is the same Cursor usage as `cursor_local`, as Cursor counted and charged it, with `costCents`. Enable one of the two, never both, or Cursor is counted twice. The dashboard sources send the user's Cursor login to `cursor.com`, so `SOURCES` leaves them out: enable them by name. `collect` asks the dashboard at most every 15 minutes and re-reads the last 7 days, because Cursor can publish a request's usage after it finished. The checkpoint moves only once the whole window is read. Besides the user's own usage, it reads each Cursor team the user belongs to and keeps only the rows that user owns, because usage billed to a team (Grok Bot's, for example) is missing from the personal read. A row both reads return counts once.

Each model turn becomes a `TokenEvent`: input, output, cache read, cache write and reasoning tokens, with session, message id, model and timestamp. Message content is never read into an event.

## Install

```sh
bun add llm-usage-extraction
```

## Use

`collect` reads every enabled source from where the last read stopped and yields batches. Commit a batch's state only after you have stored its events, so a failure re-reads them next time.

```ts
import { collect, type ExtractState } from "llm-usage-extraction";

let state: ExtractState = { files: {} };
for await (const batch of collect(state, { enabled: new Set(["claude_code", "codex"]) })) {
  await store(batch.events);
  state = batch.commit(state);
}
```

Persist `state` between runs to read only new lines. `dirs` reads only the given folders for a source instead of its default locations, for example `{ claude_code: [ownDir, otherDir] }`. `seen` replaces the set of message keys used to drop repeats within a run; a long-running process reading GBs of logs can pass a smaller one, such as `{ has: (k) => hashes.has(Bun.hash(k)), add: (k) => hashes.add(Bun.hash(k)) }`.

The parsers (`parseClaudeCodeFile`, `parseCodexFile`, `parseCursorTranscriptFile`, `parseCursorLocal`, `readOpencodeDb`, and `fetchCursorUsagePages` for the dashboard) and the file listers (`listClaudeCodeFiles(dir?)`, `listOpencodeDbs(dir?)` and friends) are exported for callers that walk other directories. A lister given a `dir` reads only that folder; with none it reads every default location.

## What it handles

- Claude Code writes one line per content block with the same message id, and only the last has the final `output_tokens`. Each message counts once, with the last line's numbers. A message split across two reads arrives twice with the same ids; keep the larger numbers.
- Codex's `input_tokens` includes cached tokens; events report them separately. Replayed `token_count` lines and the parent history copied into forked or subagent rollouts are not counted again.
- OpenCode keeps messages in SQLite: `message` in 1.x, `session_message` in 2.x, which copies older sessions over with the same ids, so each message counts once. The database is opened read-only and only ids, times, model names and token counts are selected. A reply counts once it has finished; a reply with no tokens (aborted) does not count. OpenCode's `output` leaves out reasoning, so reasoning is added back to match the other sources. Reads resume from the last `(time_updated, id)` per table, 5000 rows a batch. A message updated after it was read arrives again with the same ids.
- Session logs of several GB are read in bounded windows, and a partly written last line is left for the next read.
